newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia adds incentives to offshore centre.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia adds incentives to offshore centre.

text.p: Malaysia announced on Monday a slew of new incentives to boost investment and skills to its international offshore financial centre (IOFC) on Labuan island in the South China Sea.

Acting Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the new incentives include allowing Labuan-based banks to trade in ringgit-based instruments and maintain ringgit balances in interest-bearing external accounts.
Offshore banks would also be allowed to trade in ringgit instruments in the secondary market to allow them greater access to ringgit business and promote money market operations at the IOFC, he said.
Labuan-based banks can also now purchase ringgit instruments in the primary market using foreign currency, he said.

Labuan, located off Borneo in the South China Sea, is being modelled as a duty-free tax-haven along the lines of other successful international financial offshore centres such as Bermuda and the Cayman Islands.
Currently, 55 offshore banks and 30 offshore insurance companies have set up shop on the island.
But business has been slow to develop, analysts said.

The new incentives appear to be aimed at allowing Labuan-based firms to expand beyond foreign currency and trust operations and dabble in the domestic market, which was originally why most came to Labuan.
In insurance, Anwar said offshore life insurance companies will be allowed, starting on a date yet to be set, to sell investment-linked products to high net-worth Malaysians.
Offshore general insurance companies would also be allowed to underwrite domestic risks.

The businesses underwritten should be large with specialised risks of values exceeding 300 million ringgit, general liability risks of over 100 million ringgit ($39.8 million) and specialised liability risks valued at over 20 million, subject to conditions.
Anwar also announced new measures to attract companies and professionals to the island, including making housing and other allowances provided by employers tax exempt.
Malaysians who work on the island for a specified period of time would also be allowed to bring their cars to other parts of the country with a 50-percent reduction in custom duty.

"In order to increase the population of Labuan to generate critical mass and greater economic activities, branches of universities and institutions of higher learning will be encouraged to be set up in Labuan," Anwar said.
Labuan's population currently stands at 60,000, most of whom are still employed in fishing and agriculture.
Malaysia is also banking on its credentials as a Moslem country to attract funds from Islamic nations to Labuan.

Anwar said measures being implemented to attract Moslem funds include allowing Islamic banks, Takaful (Islamic insurance) companies and specialist Islamic financial institutions to operate on the island.

In its 1996 annual report, the Labuan Offshore Financial Services Authority said the deposits base of offshore banks based there totalled US$4.31 billion at the end of 1996, a 79 percent jump from $2.41 billion a year before.

Malaysians' share of the total deposits was at 63.7 percent at end-1996 from 78.7 percent at the end of 1995. Loans outstandings of these banks grew by 42.8 percent to $11.96 billion in 1996 over the previous year. ($ = 2.515 Malaysian Ringgits)
